title: The AI Impact Measurement Framework for Engineering Teams
summary: Measure AI's impact on engineering teams by connecting adoption, code quality, delivery speed, and developer experience to business outcomes and cost per output.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Define AI impact across adoption, output quality, delivery speed, and developer experience before selecting metrics.
- Compare the same teams, repositories, work types, and time windows before interpreting a change.
- Separate leading indicators such as adoption from lagging indicators such as delivery and defect rates; pair each signal with the outcome it should predict.
- Reject lines of code and raw suggestion acceptance counts as standalone measures. AI can inflate both without improving delivered software.
- Calculate cost per output separately from financial ROI. The first is a ratio; the second needs an evidence-backed estimate of incremental benefit.


## Why AI adoption measurement needs outcome data


AI measurement programs need to account for code produced with assistance from AI. Coding assistants can generate code, prepare commits, and increase pull request volume without producing a proportional increase in useful software. Engineering leaders can buy licenses and observe more activity while remaining unable to show whether delivery or quality improved.


Lines of code become unreliable because an assistant can produce large implementations that later require deletion or rework. Commit frequency can rise when AI tools encourage smaller, more frequent changes. Raw pull request velocity can also increase because developers can submit code faster, even when review and validation become bottlenecks. These measures capture coding activity, but they do not show whether customers received useful, reliable software.


Adoption data creates a similar problem when leaders treat usage as proof of impact. A high percentage of developers using Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex shows observed use in the covered population. Usage alone cannot show whether developers deliver changes faster, introduce fewer defects, or spend less time correcting generated code. A useful AI measurement framework must connect usage to downstream results.


[DX’s AI measurement framework](https://getdx.com/ai-measurement/) is a useful reference for connecting AI adoption with engineering outcomes. This guide takes a practical, tool-independent approach to the same measurement problem. You can apply it with existing data systems, a dedicated engineering intelligence platform, or a combination of both.


## Step 1: Define what "AI impact" means for your organization


Write down what AI impact should look like before choosing metrics. Without a shared definition, one leader may treat high tool usage as success while another expects shorter delivery cycles. A short measurement charter should identify the affected developers and expected change. It should also set an evaluation period and specify the outcomes that must not deteriorate.


Define impact across four dimensions.


- **Adoption.** Specify which developers and workflows should use AI coding assistants. A rollout may target routine code generation or test creation rather than require every developer to use AI daily.
- **Output quality.** Decide what acceptable AI-assisted work looks like. Your definition might cover escaped defects, rework, review burden, or maintainability. Higher output volume should not qualify as progress when quality declines.
- **Delivery speed.** Name the part of delivery that AI should improve. Coding assistants may reduce implementation time without changing review queues, deployment delays, or the total time required to ship a change.
- **Developer experience.** Establish whether AI should reduce repetitive work, make unfamiliar code easier to understand, or help developers complete tasks with less friction. Survey developers before rollout so you can compare later responses against a real baseline.


Your rollout stage should determine which dimensions receive the most attention. A team introducing Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex may initially focus on adoption and developer experience because delivery outcomes need time to emerge. A team with established usage should place more weight on delivery speed and output quality because continued adoption alone no longer demonstrates value.


Collecting developer experience data before rollout gives a team a comparison point for later survey results, reducing reliance on memory after rollout. The executive responsible for the rollout should approve the written definition so everyone evaluating the program uses the same intended outcomes.


## Step 2: Fix the cohort, comparison, and measurement window


Choose the people, repositories, approved tools, work types, and dates before looking at the result. Keep eligibility separate from activity: the denominator for adoption is developers who could use the tool during the period, not licenses purchased or accounts provisioned. Define what event qualifies as active use and use the same rule in every period.


Record a baseline before rollout. Compare the same cohort before and after adoption over equivalent windows; when practical, add a concurrent comparison group doing similar work without the change. Keep repository scope, output definitions, and quality observation windows constant. Document changes in staffing, project mix, release process, tool pricing, and other AI rollouts that could also explain the result.


If you only have a before-and-after view, call the result an observed change or association. Do not say the AI tool caused it. Adoption, work mix, review capacity, and delivery process can all change together, and a dashboard cannot separate those effects without a suitable comparison design.


## Step 3: Separate leading indicators from lagging indicators


A balanced scorecard uses leading indicators to detect early behavior changes and lagging indicators to test whether those changes improve engineering outcomes. Leading indicators can move within days of an AI rollout. Lagging indicators often need several delivery cycles before a meaningful pattern appears.


Leading indicators show whether eligible developers use an AI coding tool and incorporate its output. Adoption rate measures active use during a defined period, while AI-assisted PR volume tracks the number or share of pull requests created with AI support. Suggestion acceptance rate measures how often developers keep generated code. None of these metrics establishes that the accepted output improves delivery or quality.


AI can raise activity metrics without producing a comparable improvement in delivered software. Developers can accept generated suggestions that later require rework, and they can split the same change across more pull requests. Neither PR velocity nor commit frequency establishes useful output in isolation.


Lagging indicators measure the outcomes that adoption should eventually affect. Cycle time shows how long work takes to move through the delivery process. Defect rate should track a consistent quality failure, such as escaped defects. Delivery throughput counts completed changes that meet your organization’s definition of delivered value. These measures move more slowly because review capacity, release processes, and project mix can mask the effect of AI in the short term.


Pair each leading indicator with the outcome it should predict.


- Pair adoption rate with cycle time. Higher use supports the investment case only if comparable work moves through delivery faster.
- Pair AI-assisted PR volume with delivery throughput. More AI-assisted pull requests carry limited meaning when completed work stays flat.
- Pair suggestion acceptance rate with defect rate or rework. A rising acceptance rate may indicate useful suggestions, but stable or lower rework provides stronger confirmation.


Define each pair before collecting data, including the expected direction and review period. Compare developer cohorts doing similar work in comparable repositories. If adoption rises while outcomes remain unchanged, investigate review bottlenecks, task fit, and generated-code quality before expanding the rollout.


## Step 4: Watch for vanity metrics that create false confidence


Lines of code measures production volume, not delivered value. AI coding assistants can generate verbose or duplicative implementations that engineers later remove. A higher line count may therefore increase review and maintenance work without improving delivery speed or product capability. You should evaluate AI-assisted code through defects, rework, review burden, and completed outcomes instead.


Raw suggestion-acceptance counts have the same weakness. Engineers may accept large amounts of routine or temporary code while rejecting a smaller suggestion that would solve a difficult problem. Acceptance rate is a behavior signal, but by itself it does not establish whether accepted code improved delivery, quality, or business outcomes.


Goodhart’s Law describes the behavioral risk. When you turn an activity measure into a target, engineers adapt their work to improve that measure. A target based on accepted suggestions encourages acceptance, while a target based on pull request count encourages smaller or more frequent pull requests. Your measurement program should treat those figures as diagnostic signals and judge progress through the quality and delivery outcomes they are expected to predict.


## Step 5: Connect adoption, spend, output, and quality with explicit formulas


Use the same cohort and repository scope throughout. For every ratio or before-and-after comparison, record the dates, numerator, denominator, data source, and exclusions so another analyst can reproduce it. If a quality outcome needs more time to mature, set the follow-up window in advance and apply it consistently to both cohorts.


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Signal Reproducible calculation Read it alongside


Adoption Weekly active eligible developers ÷ eligible developers. Define the qualifying usage event and approved tool list. AI-attributed output and developer experience; seats alone are not use.


AI-attributed output share Output units attributed to AI ÷ all measured output units in the same cohort and window. Attribution source and coverage; native telemetry, commit metadata, and activity-based estimates have different evidentiary strength.


Delivery Choose a consistent cycle-time definition and report it with completed, valuable work per period. Work type, review queues, and release process; coding speed is only one part of delivery.


Quality Choose a stable signal, such as reverts per merged pull request, escaped defects per release, or review rework per change. The observation window and denominator; recent changes may not have mature defect data.


Spend coverage Reconciled billed AI charges represented in the measurement dataset ÷ all billed AI charges for the same billing accounts, declared tool set, and dates. Record that billing population and tool list. Keep billed actuals, allocations, modeled usage, estimates, and unassigned charges separate; if complete billing totals are unavailable, coverage is unknown.


Cost per output Attributed AI spend ÷ measured output units for the same matched developers and period. Quality, delivery, and cost coverage. This is an efficiency ratio, not a financial ROI percentage.


Calculate spend coverage over the same billing population on both sides. The share of that spending assigned to a selected engineering cohort is a separate allocation measure, not telemetry coverage. Reconcile the same billing period and currency, avoid counting included subscription usage twice, and disclose tools outside the declared scope.


Use one output unit consistently. Weave's public[AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) uses estimated expert hours of merged pull-request output for its cost-per-output-hour ratio. The public Weave Index matches engineers with both attributed AI spend and merged output in the same month; ignored pull requests and unassigned organization-level overages are excluded. The output unit estimates the effort an expert engineer would need to complete a change; it is not recorded developer time, hours saved, or the business value of the change. If you use a different output unit, label it and do not combine it with the Weave Index series.


**Velocity**


Measure end-to-end delivery speed rather than coding speed alone. Track how quickly an approved priority reaches production and provides enough evidence to decide what to do next. Cycle time provides part of that view, while delivery throughput shows how often you complete meaningful units such as releases, experiments, or resolved customer problems.


Implementation speed is only one part of delivery. If review, testing, dependencies, and product decisions remain unchanged, faster code generation may not shorten end-to-end cycle time. Track delivery speed and completed work to see whether the change reaches production.


**Quality**


Evaluate delivery gains alongside defects and the engineering effort required to correct them. For example, shorter cycle time carries less value if escaped defects consume the capacity saved during delivery. Compare quality signals before and after adoption, and segment results by team or use case so one unusually successful rollout does not hide weaker results elsewhere.


**Cost per output and financial ROI**


For an AI cost-per-output ratio, use AI tool costs divided by the output produced by the same measured cohort and period. If you also calculate fully loaded engineering cost per output, include labor in a separate, clearly labeled ratio. Raw token spend cannot answer whether a model or tool pays for itself, especially when subscription charges, shared accounts, or organization-level usage are not fully attributed.


Financial ROI is a separate calculation: **(estimated incremental benefit − total incremental cost) ÷ total incremental cost** . Define the benefit and cost categories with Finance, state how the baseline or comparison estimates the incremental benefit, and include relevant licensing, API, rollout, review, and rework costs. Do not convert estimated expert hours into saved payroll or money unless a credible evaluation shows that the capacity was actually released, avoided, or redirected to valued work. Report the assumptions and uncertainty beside the percentage.


Outcome metrics keep the scorecard useful when leadership asks what the investment changed. Each adoption metric should connect to a delivery outcome, and each delivery gain should retain its quality and cost context. Cost per output can improve while defects or delivery time worsen, so never present that ratio alone as proof of impact.


## Building this into a repeatable measurement system


Manual joins across several tools make AI impact reporting difficult to maintain. AI coding assistants record usage, while source control and delivery systems record what happened afterward. Quality scanners add another dataset. Shared developer and repository identifiers let you connect AI use with related pull requests and their quality or delivery outcomes, subject to the coverage and attribution limits of each source.


Build repeatability around a common unit of analysis, such as an AI-assisted pull request. Record the developer and repository associated with each AI-assisted pull request, along with the coding tool used. Attach the resulting quality signals and delivery outcomes to that record. A scheduled dashboard can replace monthly spreadsheet work, but someone must still own metric definitions, access controls, and data checks.


You can build these connections in a warehouse or use an engineering intelligence platform.[Weave](https://weaveos.com/) provides one implementation.[Token Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/token-intelligence) reports supported AI-tool usage and spend, with cost-source labels for provider billing, modeled usage, estimates, and allocated subscriptions.[Code Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/code-intelligence) scores pull-request output in estimated expert hours and provides reasoning for its estimates.[Engineering Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/engineering-intelligence) reports output, review activity, reverts, and delivery measures when the relevant repository and CI/CD data are connected. The[Weave AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) explains how the measures fit together, what is excluded, and why a signal labeled estimated is not the same as direct attribution. Not every prompt or tool charge can be tied to a specific merged change or engineer.


Once the measurement system produces stable internal trends, use the[AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) to review matched-cohort definitions and limits. Internal measurement should come first because inconsistent definitions make external comparisons unreliable.


## FAQs


- **How does this framework differ from DORA metrics?** DORA measures software delivery performance through indicators such as deployment frequency and change failure rate. An AI measurement framework adds usage attribution, developer experience, and code quality signals that help explain whether AI contributed to changes in delivery performance. DORA provides a useful delivery baseline, but it cannot isolate AI’s effect by itself.
- **Is cost per output the same as AI ROI?** No. Cost per output divides attributed AI spend by output for a defined cohort and period. A financial ROI percentage also needs a defensible incremental benefit, a complete cost definition, and a comparison or baseline; output estimates by themselves do not establish money saved.
- **How long before a measurement program shows useful results?** Review adoption and usage weekly, but wait until you have enough comparable completed work before interpreting delivery or quality trends. The required period will vary with release frequency and work volume. Compare similar developer cohorts and account for changes in project complexity during the evaluation period.
- **What is a reasonable AI adoption rate benchmark?** A useful adoption benchmark must reflect who has access to an approved tool and whether that tool supports their work. Language support, experience level, and task mix can all affect usage. Start with the percentage of eligible developers who use an approved tool weekly, then compare cohorts with similar work. Sustained use paired with stable or improving quality provides a better benchmark than registrations or licenses assigned.
- **How does this framework relate to DX’s published approach?**[DX’s current AI measurement page](https://getdx.com/ai-measurement/) describes adoption, costs and licenses, longitudinal and cohort analysis, and head-to-head tool evaluations. The framework here is a measurement protocol, not a test of DX or evidence that either platform produces better outcomes.
- **Should you build the measurement system or buy a platform?** Build it when you already maintain reliable usage, delivery, and quality datasets with shared developer identifiers. A platform such as[Weave](https://weaveos.com/) can bring supported usage and spend data together with output, quality, and delivery measures; verify integrations, attribution labels, and coverage for your own tools.

## Conclusion


You can evaluate AI investment only when adoption data is connected to delivery, quality, and cost outcomes. A platform can collect the data, but you still need written goals, reproducible definitions, an appropriate comparison, and explicit links between leading indicators and business outcomes. See the[AI ROI measurement methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) for Weave's formulas and limitations.


Review the framework as AI adoption and delivery constraints change. You can implement it with Weave, another platform, or your existing data stack.
